claims.text: High configurational entropy promotes uniform atomic-scale mixing in near-equiatomic, multi-element nanoparticles.
Uniform atomic-scale mixing suppresses phase separation.
Uniform atomic-scale mixing suppresses rapid elemental diffusion.
A thin, self-limiting surface oxide layer can form on the nanoparticles.
The passivating oxide layer protects the nanoparticles against chemical dealloying.
The passivating oxide layer protects the nanoparticles against coarsening.
Annealing in a mildly oxidizing atmosphere promotes oxide passivation relative to annealing in an inert atmosphere.
The proposed oxidizing-versus-inert processing comparison isolates surface passivation while maintaining baseline composition.
Atomic-scale core mixing and the presence or absence of a uniform, self-limiting oxide layer mediate high-temperature stability.
High configurational entropy minimizes the driving force for phase separation.
A thin surface oxide layer limits surface-atom mobility.
Entropy stabilization and oxide passivation act together to preserve nanoparticle structure and composition at high temperature.
Oxide-passivated, atomically mixed nanoparticles will retain structural and chemical stability better than nanoparticles processed under inert conditions.
Oxidizing annealing will produce finer compositional uniformity and greater resistance to coarsening than the baseline treatment.
The proposed stabilization applies under moderately oxidizing conditions when diffusion kinetics do not overwhelm entropy and passivation effects.
Highly oxidizing conditions may cause the proposed stabilization mechanism to break down.
Temperatures high enough to accelerate diffusion beyond the stabilizing effects of entropy and passivation may cause the mechanism to break down.

contradictions.description: The baseline is defined as as-synthesized nanoparticles receiving no passivation treatment, but the prediction and falsification experiment use inert-annealed nanoparticles as the comparator. An inert anneal is a separate thermal treatment and is not equivalent to the stated untreated baseline.

The intervention varies oxide passivation while nominally keeping composition and core entropy constant, so a null result can test the passivation contribution but cannot by itself falsify the separate claim that configurational entropy stabilizes atomic mixing. The falsification rule nevertheless treats a null passivation comparison as falsifying the combined entropy-and-passivation hypothesis.
